_source.learnerexamples_text: a private art collection; a valuable stamp collection; I'm going to buy the DVD named "Lord of the Rings" because I like it very much and want to have it in my DVD collection.

_source.definition_text: a group of things or people
_source.learnerexamples_text: There's quite a collection of toothbrushes in the bathroom.; I [wear] long t-shirts and I have a collection of sweaters.

_source.definition_text: when something is taken away from a place
_source.learnerexamples_text: rubbish collection; We need a different organisation for the waste collection.

_source.definition_text: someone who collects objects because they are interesting or beautiful
_source.learnerexamples_text: a collector of modern art; a stamp collector; Anne has been a collector for many years and she knows almost everything about Swedish stamps.

_source.definition_text: a place where students are educated when they are between 16 and 18 years old, or after they have finished school
_source.learnerexamples_text: a sixth-form college; a teacher-training college; a Naval college; She's at art college.; Everybody from our college will be here.

_source.definition_text: a word or phrase that sounds natural or correct when it is used with another word or phrase, or the combination formed when two or more words are frequently used together in a way that sounds natural
_source.learnerexamples_text: 'Heavy traffic' is a collocation.

_source.definition_text: a mark (:) used before a list, an example, an explanation, etc.
_source.learnerexamples_text: There's a colon missing in that sentence.

_source.definition_text: interesting or exciting qualities or parts
_source.learnerexamples_text: We added your story for a bit of local colour.; For an uncomplicated meal and a spot of local colour, choose the Lion's Arms at 15, Heather Lane.

_source.definition_text: red, blue, green, yellow, etc.
_source.learnerexamples_text: What's your favourite colour?; She wears a lot of bright colours.; What colour are your eyes?; Does the shirt come in any other colour?; Are the photos in colour or black and white?

_source.definition_text: with a very high score or with great success
_source.learnerexamples_text: He passed the entrance exam with flying colours.; I worked intens[ive]ly on the course and I passed with flying colours.

_source.definition_text: the colour of a person's skin, which shows their race
_source.learnerexamples_text: I don't care what colour her boyfriend is.; Since coming to England, I have been fortunate enough to meet so many people from all over the world. At first you try to see [someone] as a typical example of the country she is from, but as you get to know her better, you do not think about her race or colour any longer: it is her personality and human qualities that you are attracted to.

_source.definition_text: to affect what someone does, says, or feels
_source.learnerexamples_text: Her views are coloured by her own bad experiences.

_source.definition_text: to make something a particular colour
_source.learnerexamples_text: He drew a heart and coloured it red.; I haven't changed a lot, just my hair is now quite short and I coloured it black.

_source.definition_text: having bright colours
_source.learnerexamples_text: a colourful painting; She wears colourful clothes.

_source.definition_text: interesting and unusual
_source.learnerexamples_text: a colourful character; Computers make our modern life more colourful.

_source.definition_text: one of the blocks of print into which a page of a newspaper, magazine, or dictionary is divided
_source.learnerexamples_text: I didn't have time to read the whole article - just the first column.; To the editor, I am puzzled by the report which appeared on yesterday's page 2, second column, concerning the Westfield Music Festival.

_source.definition_text: any block of numbers or words written one under the other
_source.learnerexamples_text: the left-hand/right-hand column; Choose an adjective from Column A to use with a noun in Column B. ; Put your expenditure in column B.; A[t] the end of the course I had to complete a student questionnaire in which we had to tick in three columns, and the points were: good, adequate, needs improvement.

_source.definition_text: a tall, solid, usually stone post which is often used to support a roof or as decoration in a building
_source.learnerexamples_text: The roof of the temple was held up by a row of thick stone columns.; Nelson's Column in Trafalgar Square; There are a lot [of] columns outside and inside the restaurant, in Doric [style].

_source.definition_text: a flat piece of plastic, wood or metal with a thin row of long narrow parts along one side, which you use to tidy and arrange your hair
_source.learnerexamples_text: Has anyone seen my black comb?; I left my comb in your house.

_source.definition_text: to tidy your hair using a comb
_source.learnerexamples_text: She combed her hair and put on some lipstick.; I've been trying to comb out the knots in her hair.; I want to buy [a] mirror for my room because I need to see myself while I'm combing my hair.

_source.definition_text: a fight, especially during a war
_source.learnerexamples_text: The aircraft was shot down in combat. ; Gaza is accessible only by car and because of the terrorists setting ambushes against any car, it is very difficult to supply the villages round the combat zone with food and medication.

_source.definition_text: to try to stop something unpleasant or harmful from happening or increasing
_source.learnerexamples_text: new measures to combat the rise in crime ; Another way of combating the problem is to create recreational centres in which unemployed people can spend their time.

_source.definition_text: the mixture you get when two or more things are combined
_source.learnerexamples_text: Strawberries and cream - a perfect combination.; A combination of tiredness and boredom caused me to fall asleep.; This drug can be safely used in combination with other medicines.; Her experience and energy are a winning combination in business.; It has the winning combination of adventure in strange, far-off places, scientific discovery and humour.

_source.definition_text: to become mixed or joined, or to mix or join things together
_source.learnerexamples_text: My wages combined with your savings should just about pay for it.; The band combines jazz rhythms and romantic lyrics.; Boys wear jeans or longer shorts than girls, combined with patterned, cotton shirts.

_source.definition_text: to move or travel towards a person who is speaking or the place that they are speaking about
_source.learnerexamples_text: Come here!; She's coming this afternoon.; Look out - there's a car coming!; Can you come to my party?; If you're ever in Oxford, come and visit us.

_source.definition_text: to go somewhere with the person who is speaking
_source.learnerexamples_text: Come with me.; Come for a walk with us.; Would you like to come to the cinema with Sarah and me?; Can you come with me [to] my Friend's house [to] play game[s] tomorrow?

_source.definition_text: to arrive somewhere
_source.learnerexamples_text: Has she come yet?; When does the post come?; Hasn't his train come in yet?; When I came [to] Dorchester, th[e] town was very pretty.

_source.definition_text: to be available to buy in a particular colour, size, etc.
_source.learnerexamples_text: Do these trousers come in any other colour?; This cuddly baby doll comes with her own blanket and bottle.; It's the latest digitalized model that comes with a remote control.

_source.definition_text: to have or achieve a particular position in a race, competition, list, etc.
_source.learnerexamples_text: She came second in the 100m race.; Z comes after Y in the alphabet.; Which king came after Edward?; April comes before May.

_source.definition_text: If a dream or hope comes true, it really happens.
_source.learnerexamples_text: I'd always dreamt of owning my own house, but I never thought it would come true.; After all the problems I'd had, Oliver's birth was a dream come true.; I had been dreaming of going to London since I started learning English, and now that my dream had come true, I was overhelmed by joy and feeling very lucky.

_source.definition_text: to happen
_source.learnerexamples_text: Spring has come early.; The worst problems are still/yet to come.; The announcement came at a bad time.; But worse was yet to come!

_source.definition_text: to be very easy for someone
_source.learnerexamples_text: Singing came naturally to Louise.; After a while, it came naturally: I could use words I had never seen written, just because I had picked them up in a conversation or watching a video programme.

_source.definition_text: to be the most important person or thing
_source.learnerexamples_text: Her career always comes first.; They do not take the time to sit down and enjoy being with their family. The work comes first, and the family next.

_source.definition_text: If an idea comes to mind, you think of it.
_source.learnerexamples_text: I was thinking about who might be suitable for this job, and your name came to mind.; Positives did come from that crisis - more efficient engines, lighter vehicles and lead-free petrol are just some of the examples that come to mind.

_source.definition_text: to start to do something or to reach a state after a period of time
_source.learnerexamples_text: I have come to rely on acupuncture.; This place has come to be known as 'Pheasant Corner'.; All the things she had been believing in until then had come to mean [no]thing, as gold turns into coal.

_source.definition_text: used to say that you have just thought of something
_source.learnerexamples_text: Come to think of it, I've got two batteries that you can have upstairs.; Come to think of it, it really is quite difficult to say.

_source.definition_text: to become separated or removed from something
_source.learnerexamples_text: The book came apart in my hands.; The handle came off.; My shoelaces have come undone.; The door came open.

_source.base_text: when it comes to sth/doing sth
_source.definition_text: used to introduce a new idea that you want to say something about
_source.searchterms_text: came;come;comes;coming;when it comes to sth/doing sth
_source.learnerexamples_text: When it comes to baking cakes, she's an expert.; But when it comes to computers, they just impose some knowledge on students, without any interaction.

_source.definition_text: used to ask why or how something has happened
_source.learnerexamples_text: How come you didn't go to the party?; Off the record: How come that your reporter can print such lies when knowing they are perhaps hurting certain people in this important matter?

_source.definition_text: to start to exist
_source.learnerexamples_text: The new law comes into being next month. ; Only with knowledge of the written word were villages able to organise themselves in larger forms of government, leading from local to regional to national levels, [and] finally leading to transnational structures as they came into being mostly during the last 100 years.

_source.definition_text: to be criticized
_source.learnerexamples_text: The government has come under fire for closing the hospital.

_source.definition_text: If information about something bad comes to light, it is discovered.
_source.learnerexamples_text: She knew that the fraud would eventually come to light.; Eventually, their "lia[is]on" comes to light and Leo blames himself for the disastrous outcome of the events throughout his life.

_source.definition_text: to help someone who is in a difficult situation
_source.learnerexamples_text: I forgot my purse but Anna came to the rescue and lent me some money.

_source.definition_text: to deal with something as it happens, without planning for it
_source.learnerexamples_text: With an illness like this you just have to take every day as it comes.; We should, for once, put our [jea]lousy aside, start to appr[e]ciate what we have and take life as it comes.

_source.definition_text: to happen or start to happen
_source.learnerexamples_text: How did the idea for an arts festival come about?; Speaking of the past and its importance in our present, one cannot fail to observe that the very cumulative experience of a nation erects the foundation for our future. How does that come about?

_source.definition_text: to accept a sad situation
_source.learnerexamples_text: He still hasn't come to terms with his brother's death.; She had, at last, come to terms with her loss and although she still, deep in her heart, grieved for Michael she now knew that she could move on.

_source.definition_text: to seem to be a particular type of person or thing
_source.learnerexamples_text: He came across as shy.; Her confident manner can sometimes come across as arrogance.; All these promises just come across as a meaningless political stunt.; Tom comes across as a lively as well as a reliable person.

_source.definition_text: If an idea or emotion comes across, it is expressed clearly and people understand it.
_source.learnerexamples_text: His bitterness comes across in his poetry.

_source.definition_text: to go somewhere with someone
_source.learnerexamples_text: We're going to the cinema. Do you want to come along?; I'm really expecting you guys to come along.

_source.definition_text: to meet someone or find something by chance
_source.learnerexamples_text: He came across some of his old love letters in his wife's drawer.; Luckily, I've come across an advertisement of a well-known computer trader.

_source.definition_text: to arrive or appear at a place
_source.learnerexamples_text: A taxi never comes along when you need one.; Luckily someone came along soon afterwards and they went off to phone for an ambulance which brought us here.

_source.definition_text: to start to exist
_source.learnerexamples_text: I gave up climbing when my first child came along.; A few years went past before the second child came along, by this time the family had just moved into a new house, so the mother decided to be a h[ouse]wife and a kind of "day-mother" for the neighbours' children.

_source.definition_text: to be developing or making progress
_source.learnerexamples_text: Hassan's English is coming along well.; To my delight she is coming along all right.

_source.definition_text: to return to a place
_source.learnerexamples_text: I'll come back and pick you up in half an hour.; We've just come back from Amsterdam.; I['ll be] wait[ing] for your call, when you come back.

_source.definition_text: to harm the relationship between two or more people
_source.learnerexamples_text: I won't let anything come between me and my children.; Of course, there was the problem of religion that came between us: I was not Jewish and he was an orthodox one.

_source.definition_text: to get something, especially something that is unusual or difficult to find
_source.learnerexamples_text: Cheap organic food is still difficult to come by.; In the world we live in today, jobs have become much more difficult to come by.

_source.definition_text: If a price or a level comes down, it becomes lower.
_source.learnerexamples_text: House prices have come down recently.; Inflation is coming down.; The GDP (Gross Domestic Product) has come down from 0.3% to 0.2%.

_source.definition_text: to drop to the ground or floor
_source.learnerexamples_text: A lot of trees came down in the storm.; Our plane came down in a field.; The snow came down during the night.; Luckily, the curtain came down and the play was postponed.

_source.definition_text: to become ill
_source.learnerexamples_text: The whole family came down with food poisoning.; I must apologize for writing so late, but my sister came down with flu and I had to visit her.

_source.definition_text: If a situation, problem, decision, etc. comes down to something, then that is the thing that will influence it most.
_source.learnerexamples_text: The success of the venture comes down to the commitment of those involved.; In the end, it all comes down to the question of job satisfaction.

_source.definition_text: to enter a room or building
_source.learnerexamples_text: Do you want to come in for a cup of tea?; Hi, come in - lovely to see you!; He asked me if he could come in, and I said yes.

_source.definition_text: to be born, got from, or made in a particular place
_source.learnerexamples_text: She comes from Italy.; Where do you come from?; Some of the best wines come from France.; Does that quote come from Shakespeare?; She could hear banging coming from the room upstairs.

_source.definition_text: used to describe how someone is involved in a situation, story, or plan
_source.learnerexamples_text: We need people to help clean up, and that's where you come in.; Another measure is to encourage people to do some forms of exercise and this is where health care practitioners come in.

_source.definition_text: to be useful at some time in the future
_source.learnerexamples_text: Don't throw those jars away - they might come in handy.; There's a washer and a dryer in the basement. I'm sure they'll come in handy with your new bundle of joy and the rest of your lovely bunch.

_source.definition_text: If someone comes in for criticism, praise, etc., they are criticized, praised, etc.
_source.learnerexamples_text: He came in for a lot of criticism for his remarks.; The most important part of this process, and one of extremely great importance for the exhibition, is that he had to endure prejudice and often came in for heavy criticism.

_source.definition_text: to be useful and help someone do or achieve something, especially when there is nothing else to help them
_source.learnerexamples_text: You should keep that paint - it might come in useful.; However, I take great ex[c]eption to the view that much of our school education is a waste of time because everything we learn at school might come in useful later during our adulthood.

_source.definition_text: to happen successfully
_source.learnerexamples_text: His attempt to impress us all didn't quite come off.; There were some points in the schedule which frankly speaking didn't come off and the organization failed [in] some points as well.

_source.definition_text: to start to happen or work
_source.learnerexamples_text: The heating comes on at six in the morning.; I've got a cold coming on.; You can now also do you[r] shopping on the internet, get in contact with your bank and talk to doctors if you feel an illness coming on.

_source.definition_text: to get money from someone who has died
_source.learnerexamples_text: Just after I left university, I came into a bit of money.; Even though one might jump to the conclusion that he probably came into a fortune when his father passed away after setting up a successful business, this is not the case.

_source.definition_text: said to encourage someone to do something, especially to hurry or try harder
_source.learnerexamples_text: Come on or we'll be late!; Come on, help me to find it.

_source.definition_text: If a book, record, film, etc. comes out, it becomes available for people to buy or see.
_source.learnerexamples_text: When does their new album come out?; We're going to se[e] "Blade". It came out just yesterday.

_source.definition_text: If dirt or a mark comes out of something, it disappears when you clean it.
_source.learnerexamples_text: Will this red wine stain come out?; At the same time the sparkling, living and red-as-hell blood stain came out.

_source.definition_text: When the sun, the moon, or a star comes out, it appears in the sky.
_source.learnerexamples_text: It's really warm when the sun comes out.; When we were coming back, the sun came out.

_source.definition_text: If results or information come out, they are given to people.
_source.learnerexamples_text: The exam results come out in August.; The results finally came out at the beginning of October.

_source.definition_text: to tell people that you are homosexual
_source.learnerexamples_text: He hasn't come out to his family.

_source.definition_text: If something that you say comes out in a particular way, you say it in that way.
_source.learnerexamples_text: I wanted to tell her that I loved her, but it came out all wrong.

_source.definition_text: If something comes out of a process or event, it is one of the results.
_source.learnerexamples_text: I hope something good can come out of this mess.; I hope that the council could take all the goods for us, that we can come out of this situation well.

_source.definition_text: to become known
_source.learnerexamples_text: The truth about him will come out in the end.; Murder thrillers are supposed to keep the reader in suspense right up to the last page when the truth unexpectedly comes out.

_source.definition_text: to come to a place, move from one place to another, or move towards someone
_source.learnerexamples_text: Come over here and I'll do your hair for you.; Are your family coming over from Greece for the wedding?; I recently moved to a new house, because my wife came over from Sri Lanka.

_source.definition_text: to seem to be a particular type of person
_source.learnerexamples_text: Henry came over as a real enthusiast.; He always comes over as very honest, and even though he is ambitious the way he promotes himself is much more subtle than usually seen.

_source.definition_text: If a feeling comes over you, you suddenly experience it.
_source.learnerexamples_text: I don't usually get so angry. I don't know what came over me.; It is sometimes enough just to see a photograph of yourself shot 3 years ago and it comes to your mind, 'What on earth came over me?!'

_source.definition_text: to visit someone in their home
_source.learnerexamples_text: Come round tonight and we'll watch a video.; So would you come round and see me in August?

_source.definition_text: to change your opinion about something, or agree to an idea or a plan that you were against
_source.learnerexamples_text: I know Maria doesn't like you borrowing her car but she'll soon come round.; Fortunately, my parents finally came round to my way of thinking and I am glad to say they are most supportive.

_source.definition_text: If information, a result or a document comes through, you receive it.
_source.learnerexamples_text: Have the results of the tests come through yet?; If the divorce had come through, they would have spent whole weekends together.

_source.definition_text: to become conscious again after an accident or medical operation
_source.learnerexamples_text: When he came round, he couldn't remember what had happened.; When he came round, he was lying in a bed, surrounded by smiling women.

_source.definition_text: to manage to get to the end of a difficult or dangerous situation
_source.learnerexamples_text: We've had some hard times, but we've come through them.; Those who have managed to come through all these hard years and got the desired medals expect now to be paid back.

_source.definition_text: to be a particular total when numbers or amounts are added together
_source.learnerexamples_text: That comes to £50, please.; [If] a bill c[ame] to £1000, you would be shocked and regret what you had done.

_source.definition_text: to reach a state, or change to a different state
_source.learnerexamples_text: I was sad when the evening came to an end.; I came to the conclusion that the relationship wasn't working.; That was when the Labour party came to power.; That's why I came to the conclusion that the motorb[i]ke, together with anti-smog equipment, is the [only way] to get to work, unless you want [to] spend hours in a traffic jam.

_source.definition_text: to be in a particular part of a book, list, etc.
_source.learnerexamples_text: Hairdressers come under 'beauty salons' in the Yellow Pages.; Qui[te] a few, it seems, opted to go for places where they had previously worked. 17% from Education, 5% from Arts and science and 3% from the Science Stream, come under this category.

_source.definition_text: to experience something, often something unpleasant
_source.learnerexamples_text: We came under a lot of pressure to leave the area.; They have come under criticism from local campaigners.; This opinion is true in a sense but it also depends on how kids are brought up and what influences they came under.

_source.definition_text: to move towards someone
_source.learnerexamples_text: A young girl came up to me and asked for money.; A tall slim Soc came up and said:- "I will, Daryl old bud." It was James, Daryl's old school friend.

_source.definition_text: to be mentioned or talked about in conversation
_source.learnerexamples_text: What points came up at the meeting?; From time to time the discussion about keeping animals in zoos comes up.

_source.definition_text: If a job or opportunity comes up, it becomes available.
_source.learnerexamples_text: If some work comes up, you should take it.; I am delighted to help and advise you about the three proposals that have just come up.

_source.definition_text: When the sun or moon comes up, it rises.
_source.learnerexamples_text: We watched the sun come up over the ocean.

_source.definition_text: If a problem or difficult situation comes up, it happens.
_source.learnerexamples_text: Sorry I'm late - a problem came up with the keys.; I found it very useful that I did not have to write or read, and if a problem came up I just called the qualified teacher.

_source.definition_text: to be happening soon
_source.learnerexamples_text: My exams are coming up next month.; A holiday is coming up next month so it would be great if you could come sometime between Wednesday 27th to Saturday 30th.

_source.definition_text: to have to deal with a problem or difficulty
_source.learnerexamples_text: She came up against a lot of sexism in her first engineering job.; It is essential to get along well with your partners, otherwise you may come up against many problems, such as a loss of motivation, or even the risk of being fired.

_source.definition_text: to suggest or think of an idea or plan
_source.searchterms_text: come;come up with sth;come up with sth
_source.learnerexamples_text: She's come up with some amazing scheme to double her income.; Together with my teacher we came up with the idea of asking you to come to the college in order to give a talk about your latest book and about the experiences you have had as a novelist.

_source.definition_text: If information comes up on a computer screen, it appears there.
_source.learnerexamples_text: The images came up on the screen.; The photo instantly comes up on the screen of the computer and you can enjoy the game with the photo.

_source.definition_text: a successful attempt to become powerful, important, or famous again
_source.learnerexamples_text: She's made a comeback with her first new album for twenty years. ; He made a comeback and what a comeback!

_source.definition_text: someone who entertains people by telling jokes
_source.learnerexamples_text: Then, he went to London to become a comedian and now he is one of the [most] famous stars [in] that field.

_source.definition_text: entertainment such as a film, play, etc. which is funny
_source.learnerexamples_text: His latest film is described as a romantic comedy.; I prefer Shakespeare's comedies to his tragedies.; Everybody agreed to see that comedy with Jim Carrey and I know that you would like it.

_source.definition_text: a pleasant feeling of being relaxed and free from pain
_source.learnerexamples_text: She evidently dresses for comfort.; It's a little too hot for comfort.; Now you can watch the latest films in the comfort of your own room.; When the weather is bad, I need the comfort of my car.

_source.definition_text: something that makes your life easy and pleasant
_source.learnerexamples_text: home comforts; Good chocolate is one of life's little comforts.; Have you ever thought how our grandparents lived [in] their villages without extra home comforts?

_source.definition_text: when you have a pleasant life with enough money for everything that you need
_source.learnerexamples_text: He can afford to retire and live in comfort for the rest of his life.; Even when people sympathise with them, they always bear in mind that they are often rich children, who live in comfort.

_source.definition_text: when you feel better after being worried or sad
_source.learnerexamples_text: What she said brought me great comfort.; If I had been a "bad boy" and rec[ei]ved a spanking I would seek comfort in my brothers or sister and they would do the same.

_source.definition_text: to make someone feel better when they are anxious or sad
_source.learnerexamples_text: The family of the dead are being comforted by friends.; He kept close to Sandra and comforted her, saying this was the only choice they had and that things would be fine.

_source.definition_text: relaxed and free from pain
_source.learnerexamples_text: Are you comfortable perched on that seat?; I don't feel comfortable in high heels.; Do sit down and make yourself comfortable.; But when she started the lesson, everybody was comfortable and relaxed.

_source.definition_text: describes furniture, clothes, etc. that provide a pleasant feeling and that do not give you any pain
_source.learnerexamples_text: a comfortable bed/sofa; comfortable shoes/trousers; You should wear a T-shirt because it's comfortable to paint [in].

_source.definition_text: If you are comfortable in a situation, you do not have any worries about it.
_source.learnerexamples_text: I don't feel comfortable about leaving the children here alone.; Those children maybe they don't feel comfortable away from home.

_source.definition_text: having enough money for everything that you need
_source.learnerexamples_text: a comfortable retirement; Certainly, there are part-time jobs, but they are mostly not [so] well-paid that it would be enough for somebody to lead a comfortable life.

_source.definition_text: in a comfortable way
_source.learnerexamples_text: We slept very comfortably that night.; I was sitting comfortably on the couch watching TV when suddenly all the lights went out, [and] everything became silent.

_source.definition_text: a magazine with stories told in pictures
_source.learnerexamples_text: As a boy I used to love reading comics.; a comic book; My hobbies are play[ing] basketball and read[ing] comics.

_source.definition_text: making you feel better when you are anxious or sad
_source.learnerexamples_text: He said a few comforting words.; Furthermore, it is always very comforting to know that someone has the same or even worse problems than we do.

_source.definition_text: a mark (,) used to separate parts of a sentence, or to separate the items in a list
_source.learnerexamples_text: Put a comma before his name.

_source.definition_text: funny
_source.learnerexamples_text: a comic actor/performance; I think it's a bit long for a comic film (3 hours!!) but it's very [funny]: you must see it.

_source.definition_text: an order to do something, especially one given by a soldier
_source.learnerexamples_text: He hated being in the army because he had to obey commands.; When I give the command, fire!; Under the red lights of his command room, the first question that the captain wanted to a[sk] was to know if the boat was safe.

_source.definition_text: knowledge of a subject, especially a language
_source.learnerexamples_text: She had a good command of Italian.; Besides, I have a good command of French and I speak English fluently, which might be useful during the voyage around the world.

_source.definition_text: an instruction to a computer

_source.definition_text: so interesting or exciting that you cannot stop reading, playing, or watching it
_source.learnerexamples_text: This documentary about life in prison makes compulsive viewing.

_source.definition_text: If something is compulsory, you must do it because of a rule or law.
_source.learnerexamples_text: Wearing seat belts in cars is compulsory by law.; Swimming was compulsory at my school.; We have asked participants to wear a typical traditional dress/suit from their country - of course, this is not compulsory but everyone is warmly invited to do so.

_source.definition_text: an electronic machine that can store and arrange large amounts of information
_source.learnerexamples_text: We've put all our records on computer.; computer software/hardware; computer graphics; a computer program; computer games

_source.definition_text: to hide something
_source.learnerexamples_text: The listening device was concealed in a pen. ;  She could barely conceal her irritation. ; She had managed to conceal her dark secret from everybody.

_source.definition_text: to admit that something is true, even though you do not want to
_source.learnerexamples_text: Even the company chairman concedes that the results are disappointing. ; As a frequent user of the town library, I had to concede that the article was telling the truth.

_source.definition_text: too proud of yourself and your actions
_source.learnerexamples_text: I find him very conceited.; This is not to say that the successful person must be smug, conceited or bumptious; but he has to be convinced of his own skills and abilities.

_source.definition_text: to allow someone to have something, even though you do not want to
_source.learnerexamples_text: The government will not concede to rebel demands. ; "It's wonderful, isn't it, how you always get what you pray for." This quote, Milly's reaction when her father concedes to buying her a horse, is a good illustration of her general attitude towards religion and life.

_source.definition_text: to be able to imagine something
_source.learnerexamples_text: I cannot conceive of anything more horrible.; You cannot conceive of any other way of existence than the one you know.

_source.definition_text: to think of an idea or plan
_source.learnerexamples_text: The original idea for the novel was conceived in Rome.; I wonder what kind of person conceived this terrible and ignorant idea.

_source.definition_text: to become pregnant
_source.learnerexamples_text: She had been trying for years, but never managed to conceive.; By then she had everything she could ask for but for some reason she did not conceive for 2 years. [T]hen she conceived but had two miscarr[i]ages.

_source.definition_text: to think very carefully about something you are doing and nothing else
_source.learnerexamples_text: Come on, concentrate! We haven't got all day to do this.; I can't concentrate on my work with all that noise.; I'm going to concentrate on my writing for a while.; I can't concentrate on studying.

_source.definition_text: to be present in large numbers or amounts in a particular area
_source.searchterms_text: (be) concentrated around/in/on, etc.;be concentrated around/in/on etc;be concentrated around/in/on, etc.;concentrate;concentrated;concentrates;concentrating
_source.learnerexamples_text: Most of the fighting was concentrated in the mountains.; However it might imply a shift from large stores, concentrated in a few areas within or outside the city, to more local services.

_source.definition_text: the ability to think carefully about something you are doing and nothing else
_source.learnerexamples_text: The noise outside made concentration difficult.; There was a look of intense concentration on her face.; I find that yoga improves my powers of concentration.; I found it hard to follow what the teacher was saying, and eventually I lost concentration.; First of all, in my opinion, watching a film is more relaxing, because you don't have to concentrate to[o] much on it. You only have to watch the screen, while books require more concentration.

_source.definition_text: a principle or idea
_source.learnerexamples_text: the concept of free speech; I failed to grasp the film's central concept.; I had been trying very hard to get the point of the concept.

_source.definition_text: a large number or amount of something in the same place
_source.learnerexamples_text: high concentrations of minerals; Again, we may need to think about [the] implementation of more strict regulations related to the concentration of toxic chemicals in exhausts.

_source.definition_text: to be important to someone or to involve someone directly
_source.learnerexamples_text: Matters of pollution and the environment concern us all.; There are one or two other matters that don't concern you.; Fitness and health are two important issues in life which concern all of us.

_source.definition_text: an idea about what something is like or a way of understanding something
_source.learnerexamples_text: They have no conception of how ordinary people live.; Therefore, unless we stretch the conception of personality to cover conformity with practice and social norms, economic decisions, and the choice of identities we aspire [to], the clothes that people wear may not reflect their personality, as [this] can be conditioned by many contingencies.

_source.definition_text: to be about a particular subject
_source.learnerexamples_text: The next item on the agenda concerns staffing levels.; Your other question concerns clothes.

_source.definition_text: to worry or upset someone
_source.learnerexamples_text: What really concerns me is her lack of experience.; The fact that the coach only had broken safety belts concerned me a great deal.

_source.definition_text: when you feel worried or nervous about something, or something that makes you feel worried
_source.learnerexamples_text: Concern for the safety of the two missing teenagers is growing.; There's a lot of public concern about/over dangerous toxins recently found in food.; The situation has been causing concern for some time now.; My concern is that you're not getting enough work done.; There's a matter of some concern that I have to discuss with you.

_source.definition_text: something that is important to you, or when something is important
_source.learnerexamples_text: Our primary concern is safety.; My concern is what present to buy for Mr Brown.

_source.definition_text: worried
_source.learnerexamples_text: He's very concerned about her health.; I'm concerned that sales figures haven't improved; Concerned parents have complained about the dangerous playground.; We are getting more and more concerned about our health and how to get and keep fit nowadays.

_source.base_text: as far as sth is concerned
_source.definition_text: used to say what you are talking about
_source.searchterms_text: as far as sth is concerned;concerned
_source.learnerexamples_text: As far as money is concerned, we're doing very well.; First of all, I think the Majestic Hotel would be the right location, but I have doubts as far as the costs are concerned.

_source.base_text: as far as sb is concerned
_source.definition_text: used to say what someone's opinion is
_source.searchterms_text: as far as sb is concerned;concerned
_source.learnerexamples_text: As far as I'm concerned, feng shui is a load of rubbish.; As far as our customers are concerned, price is the main consideration.; As far as Laura was concerned, he was the most disgusting man in the world.

_source.definition_text: to be about a particular subject
_source.learnerexamples_text: The programme was more concerned with politics than the history of the place.; This field of linguistics is concerned with language acquisition.; This report is concerned with finding the best accom[m]odation for the three-day trip in north-west England.

_source.definition_text: involved in something or affected by it
_source.learnerexamples_text: A letter will be sent out to everyone concerned.; The amount of refund is to be negotiated with everyone concerned separately.

_source.definition_text: about
_source.learnerexamples_text: I've had a letter from the tax authorities concerning my tax payments.; I am writing in reply to your letter concerning the prize I won in your competition, which is two weeks at Camp California in the U.S.A.

_source.definition_text: a performance of music by one or more musicians or singers
_source.learnerexamples_text: a pop/classical concert; a school concert; To help with the concert I can sell tickets.

_source.definition_text: something that you agree to do or give to someone in order to end an argument
_source.learnerexamples_text: Both sides will have to make concessions. ; Nevertheless, I still have the impression that some concessions have to be made and from personal experience, I can say it is very different to base your choice on a single criterion.

_source.definition_text: a reduction in the price of a ticket for a particular group of people such as students, people without a job, or old people
_source.learnerexamples_text: We offer concessions to students.; At the moment, people are not very motivated to use the public transport and only children, students and pensioners get a concession card.

_source.definition_text: to decide something after studying all the information about it very carefully
_source.learnerexamples_text: The report concluded that the drug was safe.; It is because of this apparent pattern that we can conclude that as people grow older, they tend to visit the cinema less frequent[ly].

_source.definition_text: to end something such as a meeting, speech, or piece of writing by doing or saying one last thing
_source.learnerexamples_text: The concert concluded with a firework display.; I would like to conclude by thanking you all for attending.; To conclude, I would like to underline one more time how crucial the setting up of a library would be for our college.

_source.definition_text: used to introduce the last part of a speech or a piece of writing
_source.learnerexamples_text: In conclusion, I would like to thank our guest speaker for her fascinating talk.; In conclusion, swimming is an enjoyable form of exercise and an excellent way to keep fit.; In conclusion, music, TV and clothes are very important in a young person's life and can reflect each person's character.

_source.definition_text: the opinion you have after considering all the information about something
_source.learnerexamples_text: At first I thought he was a bit rude but I've come to/reached the conclusion that he's just shy.; Dear Jack and Ben: I['ve] been thinking about your last letter for quite a long time and I came to the following conclusion.

_source.definition_text: to guess the facts about a situation without having enough information
_source.learnerexamples_text: He saw them talking together and jumped to conclusions.; I think, before jumping to conclusions, we should first try to anal[ys]e the situation.

_source.definition_text: to cause you to think that something is probably true
_source.learnerexamples_text: So you thought I was leaving, did you? What led you to that conclusion?; These results lead us to the conclusion that only people with "minds tough enough" will survive.

_source.definition_text: proving that something is true
_source.learnerexamples_text: conclusive evidence/proof ; Although there is no conclusive evidence of the influence of food on people's behaviour, we can observe certain patterns of beh[a]viour depending on what kind of food people eat.

_source.definition_text: the final part of something
_source.learnerexamples_text: the dramatic conclusion of the film; The case should finally be brought to a conclusion this week.; When it comes to the crunch, he is patient and persistent enough to carry a project to a successful conclusion.

_source.definition_text: a very hard building material made by mixing together cement, sand, small stones and water
_source.learnerexamples_text: reinforced concrete; a concrete floor/path; a grey concrete building; Some of our children, brought up in modern cities, in a world of concrete, cars, motorways and supermarkets, when asked: "What is a fish?" are only able to answer: "a square piece of white flesh we take from the freezer".

_source.definition_text: in a way that proves that something is true
_source.learnerexamples_text: It is possible to prove conclusively that he was at home at the time.; This undeniable fact implies advantages that were unthinkable in the past, yet we cannot prove conclusively that the gains outweigh the losses.

_source.definition_text: certain or based on facts
_source.learnerexamples_text: They think she killed her husband, but they have no concrete evidence/proof.; We've got a general idea of what we want, but nothing concrete at the moment.; Another piece of concrete evidence to suggest that children from a poorer background cannot cope with social problems properly compared to the other group is the fact that they are more inclined to be the troublemakers themselves.

_source.definition_text: existing in a real form that can be seen or felt
_source.learnerexamples_text: concrete achievements/actions; concrete objects; In order to turn it into a feasible concept, this process of learning should be applied to concrete situations.

_source.definition_text: to say very strongly that you think something is wrong or very bad
_source.learnerexamples_text: The Prime Minister was quick to condemn the terrorists.; At first these needs were satisfied by different religions, but as we are living in a material world that does not care about spiritual things any more, we created our own idols whom we can look at, judge, admire or condemn - celebrities.

_source.definition_text: the physical situation that someone or something is in and affected by
_source.learnerexamples_text: The prisoners were kept in the most appalling conditions.; Severe weather conditions are making driving difficult.;  What are their living/working conditions like?;  Under what conditions do plants grow best?; Althoug[h] I had fun the weather conditions were horrible - it was raining all the time and the road was too wet to ride on.

_source.definition_text: the particular state that something or someone is in
_source.learnerexamples_text: My bike's a few years old, but it's in really good condition.; They left the flat in a terrible condition - there was mess everywhere.; He's in no condition to drive home.; It's very beautiful and in good condition.

_source.definition_text: only if
_source.learnerexamples_text: I'll come with you on condition that we're back before midnight.; I would like to do this on condition that you will not mention my name [on] the website.

_source.definition_text: an illness
_source.learnerexamples_text: a medical condition; He suffers from a rare heart condition.; Besides, all the fats we eat every day plus the accumulated stress of a job, makes us the perfect candidates [for] a heart condition.

_source.definition_text: something that must happen or be agreed before something else can happen
_source.learnerexamples_text: One of the conditions of the contract is that we can't keep pets.; Now I want you to pay for that as it was agreed between us and according to the terms and conditions of the contract.

_source.definition_text: to make a person or animal behave in a particular way by influencing the way they think
_source.learnerexamples_text: The boys were conditioned to be aggressive.; We are then conditioned, somehow, to choose among a restricted range of offers and products, the ones they place before our very eyes on the telly.

_source.definition_text: to organize and perform a particular activity
_source.learnerexamples_text: We are conducting a survey to find out what our customers think of their local bus service.; The experiments were conducted by scientists in New York.; This is based on a questionnair[e] conducted in the school and our English department's investigation.

_source.definition_text: to stand in front of a group of musicians and control their performance
_source.learnerexamples_text: The orchestra was conducted by Charles Miller.; The o[r]chestra conducted by Mr Miller was just superb.

_source.definition_text: to behave in a particular way
_source.learnerexamples_text: She conducted herself with great dignity.; The qualities I admire most in other people are, first of all, the ability to hide your own feelings - being a little reserved - and at the same time the ability to conduct yourself in such a way so that other people are influenced by you.

_source.definition_text: a large, formal meeting, often lasting a few days, where people discuss their work, politics, subjects they are studying, etc.
_source.learnerexamples_text: a conference on women's rights; the annual sales conference; They frequently hold conferences at the hotel.; I'm speaking at/attending a conference next week.; As you know, I went to Canada in order to take part in an environmental conference.

_source.definition_text: someone who stands in front of a group of musicians or singers and controls their performance
_source.learnerexamples_text: a famous conductor; I am fifty five years old and have experience [as] a conductor of a choir.

_source.definition_text: to admit that you have done something wrong or something that you feel guilty or bad about
_source.learnerexamples_text: She confessed to her husband that she had sold her wedding ring.; He has confessed to the murder.; He confessed to sleeping through most of the film.; I have to confess, I was a little confused at first.; I found it all very confusing, I must confess.

_source.definition_text: when you are certain of your ability to do things well
_source.learnerexamples_text: He's got the confidence to walk into a room of strangers and immediately start a conversation.; The training has given me the confidence to deal with any situation that arises.; She has ability but she lacks confidence.; I have every/complete confidence in her. She'll be perfect for the job.; As a result of such a bad appearance he lacks confidence.

_source.definition_text: when you admit that you have done something wrong or illegal
_source.learnerexamples_text: He made a full confession to the police.; I have a confession to make - I've lost that book you lent me.; I also have a confession to make.

_source.definition_text: trusting someone's ability or believing that something will produce good results
_source.learnerexamples_text: Kate's new to the job, but I've got every confidence in her.; I have every confidence in your ability to reach a compromise.

_source.definition_text: If you tell something to someone in confidence, you do not want them to tell anyone else.
_source.learnerexamples_text: I'm sorry, she told me that in confidence.; His real name isn't Piggy but he told Ralph in confidence that they called him that in school because of his appearance.

_source.definition_text: certain about your ability to do things well
_source.learnerexamples_text: Be a bit more confident in yourself!; It was a confident performance.; He feels confident of winning.; But I soon felt more confident, as I saw what activities they were doing: some people were playing tennis, others were sunbathing in the garden.

_source.definition_text: being certain that something will happen
_source.learnerexamples_text: Are you confident that enough people will attend the event?; They don't sound confident about the future of the industry.; All in all, I'm confident that a solution will be found and our town will soon regain its former attractive look.

_source.definition_text: secret, especially in an official situation
_source.learnerexamples_text: These documents are strictly confidential. ; Remember, you are under no obligation to do anything and of course we will treat the confidential information you give us with discretion and respect.

_source.definition_text: with confidence or in a confident way
_source.learnerexamples_text: Try to act confidently, even if you feel nervous.; I am quite [a] hard worker and I can confidently say that I am quite [a] reliable person.

_source.definition_text: to make an arrangement or meeting certain, often by telephone or in writing
_source.learnerexamples_text: Six people have confirmed that they will be attending and ten haven't replied yet.; Flights should be confirmed 48 hours before departure.; I've accepted the job over the phone, but I haven't confirmed in writing yet.; I just want to confirm that we're going to the ABC cinema tonight.

_source.definition_text: to prevent someone from leaving a place or to prevent something from spreading
_source.learnerexamples_text: He was confined to a prison cell for several days. ; Being Portuguese, I was confined to this small rectangle until I was a 15-year-old boy.

_source.definition_text: to say or show that something is true
_source.learnerexamples_text: His wife confirmed that he had left the house that morning.; The leader's speech was impressive and confirmed her faith in the party.; Besides, it was confirmed by scientists that consum[er]ism may develop [in]to a compulsion.

_source.definition_text: a statement, often written, that an arrangement or meeting is certain
_source.learnerexamples_text: a letter of confirmation; We've only had five confirmations for the conference so far.; We will send you written confirmation of our offer shortly.; I look forward to receiving your confirmation.

_source.definition_text: serious disagreement between people with opposing opinions or principles
_source.learnerexamples_text: There was a lot of conflict between the two parties.; The Government was in conflict with the unions over pay.; It was an unpopular policy and caused a number of conflicts within the party.; As you know I was in conflict with myself, should I buy a computer or a bicycle?

_source.definition_text: fighting between two or more groups of people or countries
_source.learnerexamples_text: armed conflict; In these years, Europe was in conflict with China, which meant war.

_source.definition_text: a situation where someone cannot make fair decisions because they are influenced by something
_source.learnerexamples_text: She resigned from the committee because of a conflict of interest.; It could become a conflict of interest, but he never lets it.

_source.definition_text: to tell someone something, or show them something to try to make them admit they have done something wrong
_source.learnerexamples_text: Confronted with the evidence, she broke down and confessed.; We had bills coming in our door, old ones which w[ere]n't paid and whenever I confronted him, he told me he would take care of it.

_source.definition_text: to be in a difficult situation, or to be shown something which may cause difficulties
_source.learnerexamples_text: We are confronted by the possibility of war.; Youngsters are confronted with a lot of difficulties and dangers and are often bound to collapse psychologically from the hard pressure on them.

_source.definition_text: to see that a problem exists and try to deal with it
_source.learnerexamples_text: First, they must confront their feelings of anger.; His inability to confront Ethan's death, as well as his being too methodical, cause[s] his wife Sarah to reconsider their marriage.

_source.definition_text: a fight or argument
_source.learnerexamples_text: She witnessed a confrontation between the two men.; There, he finds himself in a direct confrontation with Captain Beatty, the head of the fire station, who represents everything that's evil, as he knows about books but still willingly destroys them.

_source.definition_text: to think that one person or thing is another person or thing
_source.learnerexamples_text: I think you're confusing me with my sister - we look quite similar.; It's easy to confuse his films, because he tends to use the same actors.; I had confused the two words, "uvas", which means grapes, and "huevos", which means eggs and said "huevas", which unfortunately means testicles, instead...

_source.definition_text: to make someone unable to think clearly, or to make something difficult to understand
_source.learnerexamples_text: You're confusing him! Tell him slowly and one thing at a time.; Stop confusing the issue!; When the corpse was found he - successfully - tried to confuse Mrs. Marple, Scotland Yard and the members of the family where he was the doctor.

_source.definition_text: not clear
_source.learnerexamples_text: The witnesses gave confused accounts of what happened.; What can a child [think], hearing such confused explanations about animals that don't live where they s[h]ould live, that don't live how they should live.

_source.definition_text: unable to think clearly or to understand something
_source.learnerexamples_text: People keep telling me different things and I'm getting very confused.; Sorry, I'm a bit confused - are we meeting here or in town?; She seemed a bit confused about the arrangements.; At first I felt very confused.

_source.definition_text: difficult to understand
_source.learnerexamples_text: I found the instructions very confusing.; As a secret agent I was prepared [for] this sort of thing but it was surprising and confusing.

_source.definition_text: when people do not understand what is happening, what they should do or who someone or something is
_source.learnerexamples_text: There seems to be some confusion about/over who is actually giving the talk.; This caused some confusion because the courses were not completely prepared.

_source.definition_text: a situation, often with a lot of activity and noise, in which people do not know what to do
_source.learnerexamples_text: In the confusion after the bomb blast, I lost my bag.; In the confusion someone pushed her against the wall and she hurt her shoulder.

_source.definition_text: a feeling of not being able to think clearly
_source.learnerexamples_text: He could see the confusion on Marion's face.; Then I thought he recognised my confusion; therefore, he opened the box, picking up something from [it].

_source.definition_text: to tell someone that you are happy because they have done something good or something good has happened to them
_source.learnerexamples_text: I was just congratulating Ceri on winning her race.; Needless to say, everybody congratulated her and she spent all evening answering questions such as: "Why did you choose water jumping?" or "Isn't it difficult for a teenager to train five hours a day and to study?"

_source.definition_text: when something is full or blocked, especially with traffic
_source.learnerexamples_text: traffic congestion; The traffic congestion in Belo Horizonte is an issue that can't be ignored.

_source.definition_text: something that you say when you want to congratulate someone
_source.learnerexamples_text: "I passed my driving test yesterday." "Congratulations! That's fantastic."; Congratulations on your engagement!; Congratulations on your wedding.

_source.definition_text: working, used, or happening with something or someone else
_source.learnerexamples_text: Our librarians use their knowledge in conjunction with the computer network.; Therefore if the banning of private cars takes place in conjunction with development in the public transport system in that city, this whole development will [have] more advantages despite some slight difficulties at the start.

_source.definition_text: a word such as 'and', 'but', 'while' or 'although' that connects words, phrases and clauses in a sentence
to join or be joined with something else
_source.learnerexamples_text: Can I connect my printer to your computer?; Where does the cooker connect (up) to the electricity?; Has the water/electricity/gas/telephone been connected in your new place yet?; I want to buy [a] computer to play games and connect to [the] Internet as well as listen to music in my free time.

_source.definition_text: to see or show that two or more people or things are involved with each other
_source.learnerexamples_text: There is no evidence to connect him with the crime.; Happiness should not be defined as material access, it should be connected with one of the most basic human needs, love.

_source.definition_text: something that joins things together
_source.learnerexamples_text: Many companies now offer free connection to the Internet.; Moreover, some portable phones have a connection to the web, so it is easy to read newspapers if one hasn't enough money to buy [them].

_source.definition_text: when someone or something is involved with or related to someone or something else
_source.learnerexamples_text: The connection between smoking and heart disease is well known.; He has denied having any connection with the terrorists.; They're sisters, are they? I knew their surname was the same, but I never made the connection.; If you are aware of the connection between food and health you can start changing your eating habits.

_source.definition_text: used to say what something is about
_source.learnerexamples_text: I am writing in connection with the above job advertised in The Daily Press on Monday 12th February.; A man has been arrested in connection with last month's murder.; Dear Mrs Brown, I am writing in connection with a surprise birthday party for your husband, Mr Brown.

_source.definition_text: a train, bus or aircraft that leaves a short time after another arrives, so people can continue their journey
_source.learnerexamples_text: The train was half an hour late and I missed my connection.; Because of bad bus connections it's not easy to get there.

_source.definition_text: to take control of a country or to defeat people by war
_source.learnerexamples_text: The English were conquered by the Normans in 1066.; However, following imper[i]alistic politics, the Persian King Darios wanted to expand his Kingdom in Europe, so he had to conquer Greece.

_source.definition_text: the part of you that makes you feel guilty when you have behaved badly
_source.learnerexamples_text: a guilty conscience; My conscience is clear because I've done nothing wrong.; Young people have pangs of conscience and are invariably hit by pestering anxiety but they adamantly [refuse] to admit it.

_source.definition_text: always doing your work with a lot of care
_source.learnerexamples_text: a conscientious student; She is conscientious and hardworking.

_source.definition_text: to know that something is present or that something is happening
_source.learnerexamples_text: The tooth doesn't exactly hurt, but I'm conscious of it all the time.;  I think she's very conscious of being the only person in the office who didn't have a university education.;  I'm very conscious of the fact that a lot of people disagree with me.; We have to be conscious that we are destroying the world where we are living.

_source.definition_text: awake and able to think and notice things
_source.learnerexamples_text: He's still conscious but he's very badly injured.

_source.definition_text: a decision/choice/effort, etc. that you make intentionally
_source.searchterms_text: a conscious decision/choice/effort etc;a conscious decision/choice/effort, etc.;conscious;conscious decision/choice/effort, etc.
_source.learnerexamples_text: Did you make a conscious decision to lose weight?; The fairly recent possibilities of birth control allow you to make a conscious decision about having children and you can postpone that decision until well after 30.

_source.definition_text: when someone is awake and can think and notice things
_source.learnerexamples_text: He lost consciousness for several minutes.; He never regained consciousness after the accident.; He lost consciousness and lay there on the floor just in front of me.

_source.definition_text: when someone knows about something
_source.learnerexamples_text: There's a growing consciousness about environmental issues among young people.; It also springs up out of a pleasure of playing the game and a consciousness that their health matters and being fit is an important element of it.

_source.definition_text: Consecutive events, numbers, or periods of time come one after the other.
_source.learnerexamples_text: the third consecutive day of rain ; Complaints from students have been increasing for the second consecutive year, tape players are repeatedly reported not fun[c]tioning.

_source.definition_text: when all the people in a group agree about something
_source.learnerexamples_text: to reach a consensus ;  The general consensus is that we should wait and see what happens. ; In addition, as the general consensus is that young people enjoy communicating through radio programmes, I suggest there is a time when messages sent by listeners are read.

_source.definition_text: to agree to do something, or to allow someone to do something
_source.learnerexamples_text: They eventually consented to let us enter. ; Fascism is regarded as one of the worst manifestations of human nature, for it was not only a man or even a larger group of men who committed the crimes against mankind that will long remain in our minds, but a whole nation who consented in silence.

_source.definition_text: permission for someone to do something
_source.learnerexamples_text: You can't come without your parents' consent. ; The role of the council is to organise things [well] and to do so with the consent of people living in the city.

_source.definition_text: the result of a particular action or situation, especially a bad result
_source.learnerexamples_text: The ship sank with disastrous consequences.; Excessive drinking can have serious consequences for a person's health.; If you neglect your relationships like that, you'll suffer the consequences.; My work was the best because I drew a big drawing about [the] consequences of us not caring [for the] environment.

_source.definition_text: used to talk about one thing that is the result of another

_source.definition_text: not important

_source.definition_text: to start to rule or govern an area
